title: Evaluating agents: beyond a single pass/fail check
hook: An agent can reach the right final answer through a wasteful, risky or lucky path; evaluate the path, not just the destination.
inPlainWords: Judging an agent only by whether the final answer was correct can hide a risky or wasteful route it took to get there. Grade the steps it took, not just where it ended up.

useCase.title: The refund agent got the right answer, twice, two different ways
useCase.story: On a test complaint, the agent correctly refunds the order. On a near-identical complaint, it correctly refunds the order too, but only after calling the wrong customer's account first, then course-correcting. Same final grade, very different risk.

approaches.name: Grade only the final output
approaches.what: Check whether the end result, like a refund amount, matches expectations.
approaches.greatWhen: As a fast first filter across many test cases.
approaches.avoidWhen: Used alone, since it can't tell a clean run from a risky one that happened to land right.
approaches.example: Both runs above pass, hiding the wrong-account call.

approaches.name: Grade the trajectory, step by step
approaches.what: Check the sequence of tool calls and decisions the agent made, not just the ending.
approaches.greatWhen: The path matters for cost, risk or compliance, not just correctness.
approaches.avoidWhen: The task is simple enough that any working path is equally fine.
approaches.example: The wrong-account call shows up as a flagged step, even though the final refund was correct.

approaches.name: Test with adversarial and edge-case scenarios
approaches.what: Deliberately include ambiguous, conflicting or malicious inputs in the test set.
approaches.greatWhen: The agent has access to real actions, like refunds or account changes, where a bad path has real cost.
approaches.avoidWhen: Skip this only for read-only, low-stakes agents.
approaches.example: A complaint with an intentionally ambiguous order number.

approaches.name: Track cost and step count, not just correctness
approaches.what: Measure how many tool calls, how much time and how much it cost to reach the answer.
approaches.greatWhen: The same task could be solved in 2 steps or 12, and that difference matters.
approaches.avoidWhen: Cost is negligible and step count doesn't affect risk.
approaches.example: One path resolves a complaint in 3 tool calls; another takes 11 for the same outcome, at 4x the cost.

approaches.name: Re-run tests after every prompt or tool change
approaches.what: Treat the agent's test set like a regression suite, run automatically before shipping any change.
approaches.avoidWhen: Never skip; small prompt tweaks can quietly change the agent's whole path.
approaches.example: A one-line prompt edit is tested against the full trajectory suite before merging.

challenge.question: Two test complaints both end in a correct refund, but one path included an unnecessary wrong-account lookup. What does grading only the final output miss?

options.text: Whether the trajectory itself was safe and efficient, not just whether the ending was correct
options.why: A correct ending can hide a risky or wasteful path; trajectory-level grading catches what output-only grading can't.

options.text: Nothing; if the final answer is correct, the path doesn't matter
options.why: The wrong-account call is a real risk, touching the wrong customer's data, even though it didn't change the final result this time.

options.text: Whether the response was worded politely
options.why: Tone matters for quality, but it's a separate concern from the safety and efficiency of the agent's actions.

options.text: Whether the test suite has enough test cases
options.why: Test coverage matters generally, but doesn't address what this specific pair of runs reveals.

bestCase.title: Trajectory grading catches the risky path
bestCase.example: The evaluation flags the wrong-account lookup even though the refund was correct, the team traces it to an ambiguous tool description, fixes it, and re-running confirms both test cases now take the clean path.

worstCase.title: A risky habit hiding behind correct answers
worstCase.example: Only final outputs are graded. The wrong-account lookup pattern ships to production, and a month later it touches a real customer's account on a genuinely ambiguous case, with no correct final answer to hide it that time.

steps.label: Run both test cases
steps.goes: Both end in a correct refund for the right order.

steps.label: Grade final output only
steps.goesWrong: The evaluation stops here, so the risky path in test case two ships unnoticed.

steps.label: Grade the trajectory
steps.goes: Test case two shows an extra call to the wrong customer's account.

steps.label: Trace the cause
steps.goes: An ambiguous tool description let the agent guess wrong before correcting.

steps.label: Fix and re-test
steps.goes: The tool description is clarified; both cases now take the clean path.

steps.label: Add to the regression suite
steps.goes: This scenario runs automatically before every future change.

takeaway: Grade the agent's trajectory, cost and safety, not just whether the final answer happens to be correct; a right answer can hide a risky path.
